question: What is the core exercise approach in physiotherapy for reducing falls among community-dwelling older adults?
gold_answer: Multicomponent exercise should be provided, and the program must include balance training; other exercise modes may also be included. The guideline classifies this as Level I evidence and a strong recommendation.
gold_passage: “Physical therapists must provide or prescribe multicomponent exercise to older adults to reduce risk and rate of falls and it must include balance training and may include other exercise modes.”

develop a clinical practice guideline (CPG) synthesizing the evidence for physical therapy management of fall risk in communitydwelling older adults. The GDG consisted of five physical therapists with clinical expertise in the management of fall risk in older
adults and methodological expertise in evidence-based document development. The CPG includes a systematic review of
existing literature, and stringent methodology developed by the
American Physical Therapy Association to form the evidencebased recommendations. The CPG content, including methodology, recommendations and algorithm were externally
reviewed by clinical providers and academicians with expertise in
fall risk management for older adults. These recommendations
are intended to assist physical therapists and physical therapist
assistants who are engaged in fall risk management for
community-dwelling older adults.
Key Words: fall risk, guidelines, older adults

(J Geriatr Phys Ther 2025;48(2):62-87.)

CLINICAL IMPLICATIONS
• Physical therapists can use the evidence-based algorithm to facilitate clinical reasoning in the management
of fall risk for older adults.
• Multicomponent exercise is the most important intervention for addressing falls and fall risk in older adults.
• Multicomponent exercise must include progressive and
challenging balance training exercises and may include
other types of exercise.

SUMMARY OF GRADED RECOMMENDATIONS
This clinical practice guideline (CPG) provides recommendations for the management of fall risk in communitydwelling adults aged 65 and over (subsequently referred
to as older adult(s)). Multifactorial management programs
include screening, assessment, referral to appropriate providers, and interventions within physical therapist (PT) and
physical therapist assistant (PTA) scope of practice. This
guideline strongly recommends that PTs and PTAs

Recommendation
Physical therapists must provide or prescribe multicomponent exercise to older adults to reduce risk and rate for
falls and it must include balance training and may include
other exercise modes. (Evidence Quality/Level: I, Rec.
Strength: Strong) Rationale
For older adults at lower risk for falls, physical therapists
must ensure participation in a multicomponent exercise regimen that includes balance exercise to manage fall risk. For
older adults with identified impairments in strength and
balance, physical therapists must provide tailored, progressive exercise to address these deficits. This strong recommendation is based on Level 1 evidence from 14 high
or moderate quality SRs of multicomponent exercise
programs,13,14,28,34,44,45,55-57,59-63 10 additional high or
moderate quality SRs of mixed single and multi-component
exercise programs,13,14,28,36,39,46,55-57,61 and 4 lower quality
SRs that did not include meta-analysis.64-67 Details and
estimates of rate and risk reduction can be found in
Table 5 for mixed multicomponent and single component
studies, and Table 6 for multicomponent studies.

Education (V) and Environmental Modifications (A,I): should be provided specifying actions to address identified risk factors including
home hazards and strength/balance impairments, and should also include referral to appropriate providers for risk factors outside of PT
scope of practice. Provide risk-specific guidance regarding walking exercise programs for those at high risk.

Multicomponent Exercise Dosage: Provided in group or individual delivery format, for at least 3 hours/week and total volume > 50 hours
over 6-12 months. Must include balance training component.
Balance Training Dosage: Progressively reduce the BOS, movement of the body within and beyond the BOS through reaching, voluntary
stepping to adapt gait and prevent falling, and reactive stepping in response to an external perturbation to balance, reduce reliance on
upper limb support, 3+ hours/week and total volume of >50 hours.
Tai Chi Dosage: Provided 3+ times/week for a total volume of 30-60 hours.

Physical therapists should participate in multifactoriala management programs addressing falls and fall risk for older adults. | I | Strong
Physical therapists must provide or prescribe multicomponentb exercise to older adults to reduce risk and rate of falls and it must include balance training and may include other exercise modes. | I | Strong
Physical therapists must prescribe exercise programs to older adults to be performed at least 150 minutes to 3 hours per week, lasting from 6 to 12 months, and must include progressive and sufficiently challenging balance training. | I | Strong
Physical therapists must provide or prescribe balance training to older adults that is progressive and sufficiently challenging as evidenced by movement of the limbs and whole body in multiple directions, changing the base of support, and reducing upper limb support either alone or as part of a multicomponent program to reduce the risk and rate of falls. | I | Strong
Balance training must include volitional step training and/or gait adaptability training. | I | Strong
Balance training may also include reactive step (perturbation) training. | II | Weak
Physical therapists should NOT provide or prescribe resistance training ALONE to older adults if the purpose is to reduce the risk and/or rate of falls. | II | Moderate
Physical therapists should prescribe Tai Chi for older adults to reduce the risk and rate of falls. | I | Strong
Physical therapists should NOT provide education ALONE to older adults to reduce the risk and/or rate of falls. | I | Strong
Physical therapists should provide tailored education combined with individualized exercise intervention to older adults. The tailored education should include specific actions to address identified risk factors, including home hazards and strength and balance impairments, and should also include referral to appropriate providers for risk factors outside of PT scope of practice. | V | Expert opinion
Physical therapists should provide environmental assessment and recommend modifications to older adults at high risk of falls. | I | Strong

Physical therapists must provide or prescribe balance training to older adults that is progressive and sufficiently challenging as evidenced by movement of the limbs and whole body in multiple directions, changing the base of support, and reducing upper limb support either alone or as part of a multicomponent program to reduce the risk and rate of falls.
Balance training must include volitional step training and/or gait adaptability training.

Physical therapists should provide tailored education combined with individualized exercise intervention to older adults. The tailored education should include specific actions to address identified risk factors, including home hazards and strength and balance impairments, and should also include referral to appropriate providers for risk factors outside of PT scope of practice.
Physical therapists should provide environmental assessment and recommend modifications to older adults at high risk of falls.

aMultifactorial management includes screening, assessment, referral to appropriate provider, and interventions within physical therapist scope of practice. bMulticomponent exercise refers to exercise that includes more than one category of exercise according to the PROFANE1 taxonomy (balance and functional, flexibility, resistance training, 3-D).

metadata.embedding_text:
Delivery personnel
In two high-quality SRs, Sherrington compared multicomponent interventions that were delivered by health
care professionals versus non-health care professionals,
and found no difference in fall rate or fall risk between
delivery by health care professionals and by non-health
care professionals.14,28 One low-quality SR without metaanalysis66 found that most physical therapist-led group
exercise programs reduced fall rates, but not more than
individualized physical therapy programs. These results
should be interpreted with caution as it is unclear if the
samples in these studies were similar enough to make
a direct comparison or were generalizable to a wider
population. For example, older adults who participate in
a community-based program delivered by a non-health
care professional might have less frailty or more ability
to exercise independently than those who participate in
programs delivered by a physical therapist or other health
care professional.

High-risk vs low-risk older adults
The evidence on the effect of multicomponent exercise on
older adults identified as being at a higher risk vs lower
risk of falling does not allow for separate recommendations. Gillespie et al34 found a similar reduction in fall rate
in studies that selected for people at high risk of falls and
in studies that did not (30% vs 28% rate reduction).
Sherrington et al14 also reported no differences between
studies that recruited older adults selected for high risk
and those that did not (24% vs 22% rate reduction,
respectively). In contrast, in one moderate-quality SR
that examined home-based individualized exercise programs, there was no effect on fall risk when including
studies of people who were recently discharged from the

hospital, but a 16% risk reduction when those studies
were excluded.61 Because this moderate quality study is
focused on home therapy alone, the GDG does not believe
that this study provides enough evidence of a differential
effect between people at higher and lower risk.

Two SRs with meta-analysis44,60 found large reductions in the fall rate and risk when including only studies
that recruited individuals with health conditions that
might impact falls. Liu et al,60 in a moderate quality
review that included only people with reduced physical
capacity, found a 37% reduction in fall rate, and Petridou
et al44 found an even larger 55% reduction in the fall risk
when examining studies that included only people with
a history of falls. Thus, we are unable to make separate
recommendations about high-risk individuals vs the general population and recommend that physical therapists
use clinical judgment based on individual patient examination of the movement system, patient safety, and
patient preferences.

Statement of Intent
This document is intended to guide primarily physical
therapists and physical therapist assistants in the management of fall risk in older adults. Secondarily, this CPG
may provide guidance to older adults, family members,
educators, researchers, policymakers, and payers. It is not
intended to be construed or to serve as a legal standard of
care or as an insurance benefit determination document.
As rehabilitation knowledge expands, CPGs are promoted as syntheses of current research and provisional
proposals of recommended actions under specific conditions. Standards of care are determined based on all clinical data available for an individual patient/client and are
subject to change as knowledge and technology advance,
patterns of care evolve, and patient/family values are integrated. This CPG is a summary of practice recommendations that are supported by current published literature
that has been reviewed by expert practitioners and other
interested parties. These parameters of practice should be
considered guidelines only, not mandates. Adherence to
them will not ensure a successful outcome for every
patient, nor should they be construed as including all
proper methods of care or excluding other acceptable
methods of care aimed at the same results.

This CPG includes interventions provided in group settings and in individual one on one clinical settings. Some
older adults can exercise without supervision in group
settings, while others may need one-on-one intervention
to safely exercise. Individualized exercise prescription
should be driven by a targeted PT examination and evaluation of the movement system to identify impairments that
contribute to the risk identified with performance based
and self-report measures. Recommendations for specific
examination tests and measures to support individualized
exercise prescription are outside the scope of this CPG.

The ultimate decision regarding a particular clinical
procedure or treatment plan must be made using the
clinical data presented by the patient/client/family, the
diagnostic and treatment options available, the patient’s
values, preferences, expectations, support, and resources,
and the clinician’s scope of practice and expertise. The
CPG suggests that significant departures from accepted
guidelines should be documented in patient records at the
time the relevant clinical decisions are made.

METHODS
The American Physical Therapy Association-Geriatrics
(APTA-Geriatrics) is an Academy of the American
Physical Therapy Association that serves physical therapists, physical therapist assistants, and students who
work with older adults. The APTA-Geriatrics appointed
the members to the GDG to develop and disseminate an
evidence-based document on the management of falls.
The GDG developed the current CPG using a multipronged approach by incorporating published results
from the Geri-Edge Task Force SR13 and the previously

Recommendation: Dosage, Intensity, and Components
Physical therapists must prescribe exercise programs to
older adults to be performed at least 150 minutes to
3 hours per week, lasting from 6 to 12 months, and
must include progressive and sufficiently challenging
balance training. (Evidence Quality/Level: I, Strength:
Strong)

Rationale
Multicomponent exercise programs that include more
than 150 minutes of exercise weekly are most effective
in reducing fall rates48 and programs of 6 to 12 months
duration are most effective in reducing fall rate and risk.60

Evidence from one meta-analysis61 examining the most
effective combination of exercises in studies with longer
follow-up times indicated that the most effective combination reduced risk by 35%, and included all categories of
exercise combined, including gait, balance, and functional
training, resistance training, flexibility exercises, and 3D
training such as Tai Chi or dance.

Evidence Synthesis
Duration, intensity, and components of mixed singleand multi-component exercise programs
In three separate SRs, Sherrington et al13,14,54 investigated
the intensity, duration, and components of mixed singleand multi-component exercise interventions and found
that the highest rate reductions were found with programs
that included high intensity/high challenge balance training, did not include walking programs, had doses greater
than 50 hours, and had frequencies greater than 3 hours
per week. Differences in fall risk and rate reduction
according to duration, intensity, or exercise components
are summarized in Table 7. The most recent high-quality
SR14 showed a 50% reduction in falls in programs that
included more than 3 hours per week and balance and
functional training.

interacting in their environment without substantial
physical, cognitive or social support. Clinicians should

participate in multifactorial management programs
addressing falls and fall risk for older adults. A multifactorial approach to fall risk management in older
adults is supported by robust evidence (Evidence
Quality/Level: I, Recommendation Strength: Strong).
A multicomponent exercise program that incorporates
balance training and other modes of exercise, such as
resistance training or Tai Chi, is strongly recommended
for reducing the risk and rate of falls (Evidence Quality/
Level: I, Recommendation Strength: Strong). The guideline
strongly recommends that balance training interventions
be progressive and sufficiently challenging, involve limb
and whole-body movements, changes in base of support,
and reduced upper limb support (Evidence Quality/Level: I,
Recommendation Strength: Strong). Additionally, Tai Chi
is strongly recommended for older adults in particular
those at lower fall risk (Evidence Quality/Level: I,
Recommendation Strength: Strong). The guideline makes
a strong recommendation for environmental assessments
and necessary modifications for older adults at higher risk
(Evidence Quality/Level: I, Recommendation Strength:
Strong). Providing or prescribing resistance training
ALONE to reduce fall risk and rate is not recommended,
as it offers limited benefits.(Evidence Quality/Level: II,
Recommendation Strength: Moderate).

This guideline also provides several weak recommendations. While reactive step (perturbation) training is
a potential component of balance training, the evidence
supporting this intervention is mixed (Evidence Quality/
Level: II, Recommendation Strength: Weak) in comparison to strong evidence for volitional step training or balance training. Additionally, this guideline recommends
a comprehensive approach that combines tailored education with individualized exercise intervention, addressing
identified risk factors, home hazards, strength and balance impairments, and referral to other providers when
necessary, especially for factors outside the scope of physical therapy (Evidence Quality/Level: V, Recommendation
Strength: Expert Opinion). The recommendation for this
comprehensive approach is predicated upon expert opinion, but each individual component is recommended
based upon robust evidence. These recommendations collectively guide physical therapists in adopting evidencebased practices to manage fall risk, while also highlighting
the limitations and areas requiring further research.

et al49 also reported that when multifactorial interventions

not have a significant effect on fall rate.

High-risk versus low-risk participants
Subgroup analyses from Gates et al43 revealed that
multifactorial interventions are effective for reducing
fall rate by 23% for people at higher risk of falls but
no effect was found in studies that did not select for
people at higher risk of falls. Meta-analysis from
Caristia et al48 showed that multifactorial interventions lasting less than 12 months were effective in
reducing falls, while those lasting more than 12 months

were not. Cheng et al46 conducted a network metaanalysis (NMA) of the comparative effectiveness of
interventions and found multifactorial intervention
compared to usual care had the greatest efficacy
(36% reduced odds) relative to several other intervention comparisons including exercise, referral, and education. However, Cheng’s definition of multifactorial
intervention resulted in inclusion of multi-component
exercise interventions that likely caused overestimation
of the effect.

produced by skeletal muscles that results in energy

focus on exercise as opposed to physical activity, as
defined above. In 2018, the USPSTF released a final
statement recommending exercise to prevent falls in

ALONE to reduce fall risk and rate is not recommended,
as it offers limited benefits.(Evidence Quality/Level: II,
Recommendation Strength: Moderate).

This guideline also provides several weak recommendations. While reactive step (perturbation) training is
a potential component of balance training, the evidence
supporting this intervention is mixed (Evidence Quality/
Level: II, Recommendation Strength: Weak) in comparison to strong evidence for volitional step training or balance training. Additionally, this guideline recommends
a comprehensive approach that combines tailored education with individualized exercise intervention, addressing
identified risk factors, home hazards, strength and balance impairments, and referral to other providers when
necessary, especially for factors outside the scope of physical therapy (Evidence Quality/Level: V, Recommendation
Strength: Expert Opinion). The recommendation for this
comprehensive approach is predicated upon expert opinion, but each individual component is recommended
based upon robust evidence. These recommendations collectively guide physical therapists in adopting evidencebased practices to manage fall risk, while also highlighting
the limitations and areas requiring further research.

metadata.embedding_text:
Limitations in study design and reporting limit the
ability to fully elucidate the importance of resistance
training for falls. No studies were stratified by risk of
falls, bias risk was consistently moderate-to-high, studies
were limited by relatively small sample sizes, and resistance
exercise was not commonly separated from multicomponent exercise protocols. Multicomponent protocols found
no effect on fall rate when either moderate or high-intensity
resistance training was included.54 Multimodal exercise
that included resistance training was analyzed in a recent
meta-analysis of RCT and found no effect on fall rate or
fall risk.76

The multicomponent or multimodal design of RCTs
and subsequent meta-analyses limits the ability to distinguish the impact of resistance training alone. A systematic
investigation with meta-analysis of the effectiveness of
resistance training as a single modality or part of a multimodal program in reducing fall rate or fall risk would
support recommendations in this area. Furthermore, the
effectiveness of unsupervised home-based resistance training programs in reducing falls has not been confirmed by
existing SRs.75

TAI CHI
In this CPG, Tai Chi refers to any form of Chinese martial
art consisting of a series of slow, low-impact, bodily
movements. One form, Yang-style, includes 24 different
forms that incorporate multidirectional weight shifting,
awareness of body alignment, and multisegmental movement coordination. Tai Chi is often included as a 3D
exercise in the ProFaNE taxonomy.1 The evidence comes
from SRs and meta-analyses that report the effect of Tai
Chi on fall risk and fall rate.

metadata.embedding_text:
Tai Chi is most often delivered in a group setting and
by trained instructors such as a Tai Chi practitioner.
Physical therapists can provide Tai Chi if they are trained
instructors.

We placed a high value on the group exercise nature of
Tai Chi. Most included studies used a version of Yangstyle Tai Chi. One SR determined Yang style may have
a greater effect on fall risk and rate than Sun style.81

However, the analysis for Sun style was based on only
three studies and this analysis may be influenced by publication bias. Therefore, we did not provide a recommendation on the style of Tai Chi to be used.

While there are benefits for older adults participating
in community-based Tai Chi intervention programs,
availability, and cost of programming along with patient
preference related to the type of exercise should be considered. Older persons may inquire about and physical
therapists should inform older adults of intervention
options if there are Tai Chi programs in their geographic
vicinity.

The GDG placed value on Tai Chi as an effective intervention for reducing fall rate and fall risk in older adults, in
particular, the GDG valued Tai Chi as an intervention for
those at lower risk of falling. Due to evidence variability,
the GDG intentionally refrained from prescribing specific
dosing and Tai Chi style recommendations. Patient preferences were recognized as crucial, considering factors such
as program availability and cost.

Evidence Synthesis
Tai Chi resulted in a 29% to 48% reduction in fall rate
and a 20% to 43% reduction in fall risk. Risk and rate
ratios varied according to the type of Tai Chi, fall risk
status of the participants, time of follow-up, and type of
control group. Estimates of fall risk and rate reduction for
studies that included Tai Chi or dance are found in
Table 12.

Higher vs lower risk of falls
There is an abundance of evidence that the magnitude of
effect is greater for persons designated as lower risk of
falling, nevertheless, persons at higher risk may benefit
from Tai Chi. The definitions of higher and lower risk of
falling varied among SRs and no standard definition could
be ascertained from the evidence.

Tai Chi is an effective intervention strategy for reducing rates of falls and fall risk in older persons living in the
community who are high functioning or have a lower fall
risk. In studies in which participants were not stratified or

selected according to risk level, fall rate reductions ranged
from 19% to 49%. Similarly, fall risk reductions ranged
from 20% to 42%. Specifically, Sherrington et al14 demonstrated a 19% rate reduction and Gillespie et al34 reported
a 41% rate reduction while Logghe et al84 reported a 49%
average reduction in fall rate.

Recommendation: Dosage, Intensity, and Components
Physical therapists must prescribe exercise programs to
older adults to be performed at least 150 minutes to
3 hours per week, lasting from 6 to 12 months, and
must include progressive and sufficiently challenging
balance training. (Evidence Quality/Level: I, Strength:
Strong)

Rationale
Multicomponent exercise programs that include more
than 150 minutes of exercise weekly are most effective
in reducing fall rates48 and programs of 6 to 12 months
duration are most effective in reducing fall rate and risk.60

Evidence from one meta-analysis61 examining the most
effective combination of exercises in studies with longer
follow-up times indicated that the most effective combination reduced risk by 35%, and included all categories of
exercise combined, including gait, balance, and functional
training, resistance training, flexibility exercises, and 3D
training such as Tai Chi or dance.

Evidence Synthesis
Duration, intensity, and components of mixed singleand multi-component exercise programs
In three separate SRs, Sherrington et al13,14,54 investigated
the intensity, duration, and components of mixed singleand multi-component exercise interventions and found
that the highest rate reductions were found with programs
that included high intensity/high challenge balance training, did not include walking programs, had doses greater
than 50 hours, and had frequencies greater than 3 hours
per week. Differences in fall risk and rate reduction
according to duration, intensity, or exercise components
are summarized in Table 7. The most recent high-quality
SR14 showed a 50% reduction in falls in programs that
included more than 3 hours per week and balance and
functional training.

This CPG addresses the management of falls and fall

a few examples. This CPG specifically defines community-dwelling older adults as 65 or over who do not
have major health conditions that prevent them from
interacting in their environment without substantial
physical, cognitive or social support. Clinicians should
use their clinical judgment for whether these recommendations apply to their patients that fall outside these

participate in multifactorial management programs
addressing falls and fall risk for older adults. A multifactorial approach to fall risk management in older
adults is supported by robust evidence (Evidence
Quality/Level: I, Recommendation Strength: Strong).
A multicomponent exercise program that incorporates
balance training and other modes of exercise, such as
resistance training or Tai Chi, is strongly recommended
for reducing the risk and rate of falls (Evidence Quality/
Level: I, Recommendation Strength: Strong). The guideline
strongly recommends that balance training interventions
be progressive and sufficiently challenging, involve limb
and whole-body movements, changes in base of support,
and reduced upper limb support (Evidence Quality/Level: I,
Recommendation Strength: Strong). Additionally, Tai Chi
is strongly recommended for older adults in particular
those at lower fall risk (Evidence Quality/Level: I,
Recommendation Strength: Strong). The guideline makes
a strong recommendation for environmental assessments
and necessary modifications for older adults at higher risk
(Evidence Quality/Level: I, Recommendation Strength:
Strong). Providing or prescribing resistance training
ALONE to reduce fall risk and rate is not recommended,
as it offers limited benefits.(Evidence Quality/Level: II,
Recommendation Strength: Moderate).

This guideline also provides several weak recommendations. While reactive step (perturbation) training is
a potential component of balance training, the evidence
supporting this intervention is mixed (Evidence Quality/
Level: II, Recommendation Strength: Weak) in comparison to strong evidence for volitional step training or balance training. Additionally, this guideline recommends
a comprehensive approach that combines tailored education with individualized exercise intervention, addressing
identified risk factors, home hazards, strength and balance impairments, and referral to other providers when
necessary, especially for factors outside the scope of physical therapy (Evidence Quality/Level: V, Recommendation
Strength: Expert Opinion). The recommendation for this
comprehensive approach is predicated upon expert opinion, but each individual component is recommended
based upon robust evidence. These recommendations collectively guide physical therapists in adopting evidencebased practices to manage fall risk, while also highlighting
the limitations and areas requiring further research.

Recommendation: Dosage, Intensity, and Components
Physical therapists must prescribe exercise programs to
older adults to be performed at least 150 minutes to
3 hours per week, lasting from 6 to 12 months, and
must include progressive and sufficiently challenging
balance training. (Evidence Quality/Level: I, Strength:
Strong)

Rationale
Multicomponent exercise programs that include more
than 150 minutes of exercise weekly are most effective
in reducing fall rates48 and programs of 6 to 12 months
duration are most effective in reducing fall rate and risk.60

Evidence from one meta-analysis61 examining the most
effective combination of exercises in studies with longer
follow-up times indicated that the most effective combination reduced risk by 35%, and included all categories of
exercise combined, including gait, balance, and functional
training, resistance training, flexibility exercises, and 3D
training such as Tai Chi or dance.

Evidence Synthesis
Duration, intensity, and components of mixed singleand multi-component exercise programs
In three separate SRs, Sherrington et al13,14,54 investigated
the intensity, duration, and components of mixed singleand multi-component exercise interventions and found
that the highest rate reductions were found with programs
that included high intensity/high challenge balance training, did not include walking programs, had doses greater
than 50 hours, and had frequencies greater than 3 hours
per week. Differences in fall risk and rate reduction
according to duration, intensity, or exercise components
are summarized in Table 7. The most recent high-quality
SR14 showed a 50% reduction in falls in programs that
included more than 3 hours per week and balance and
functional training.

metadata.embedding_text:
develop a clinical practice guideline (CPG) synthesizing the evidence for physical therapy management of fall risk in communitydwelling older adults. The GDG consisted of five physical therapists with clinical expertise in the management of fall risk in older
adults and methodological expertise in evidence-based document development. The CPG includes a systematic review of
existing literature, and stringent methodology developed by the
American Physical Therapy Association to form the evidencebased recommendations. The CPG content, including methodology, recommendations and algorithm were externally
reviewed by clinical providers and academicians with expertise in
fall risk management for older adults. These recommendations
are intended to assist physical therapists and physical therapist
assistants who are engaged in fall risk management for
community-dwelling older adults.
Key Words: fall risk, guidelines, older adults

(J Geriatr Phys Ther 2025;48(2):62-87.)

CLINICAL IMPLICATIONS
• Physical therapists can use the evidence-based algorithm to facilitate clinical reasoning in the management
of fall risk for older adults.
• Multicomponent exercise is the most important intervention for addressing falls and fall risk in older adults.
• Multicomponent exercise must include progressive and
challenging balance training exercises and may include
other types of exercise.

SUMMARY OF GRADED RECOMMENDATIONS
This clinical practice guideline (CPG) provides recommendations for the management of fall risk in communitydwelling adults aged 65 and over (subsequently referred
to as older adult(s)). Multifactorial management programs
include screening, assessment, referral to appropriate providers, and interventions within physical therapist (PT) and
physical therapist assistant (PTA) scope of practice. This
guideline strongly recommends that PTs and PTAs

Physical therapists must provide or prescribe multicomponent exercise to older adults to reduce risk and rate for
falls and it must include balance training and may include
other exercise modes. (Evidence Quality/Level: I, Rec.
Strength: Strong) Rationale
For older adults at lower risk for falls, physical therapists
must ensure participation in a multicomponent exercise regimen that includes balance exercise to manage fall risk. For
older adults with identified impairments in strength and
balance, physical therapists must provide tailored, progressive exercise to address these deficits. This strong recommendation is based on Level 1 evidence from 14 high
or moderate quality SRs of multicomponent exercise
programs,13,14,28,34,44,45,55-57,59-63 10 additional high or
moderate quality SRs of mixed single and multi-component
exercise programs,13,14,28,36,39,46,55-57,61 and 4 lower quality
SRs that did not include meta-analysis.64-67 Details and
estimates of rate and risk reduction can be found in
Table 5 for mixed multicomponent and single component
studies, and Table 6 for multicomponent studies.

Loureiro et al,49 in an acceptable quality SR, reported that

falls risk home assessment and exercise with health education showed a significant reduction in fall rate. Loureiro
et al49 also reported that when multifactorial interventions
included exercise, utilization of group exercise resulted in
reduction in fall rate, while individual exercise programs did
not have a significant effect on fall rate.

High-risk versus low-risk participants
Subgroup analyses from Gates et al43 revealed that
multifactorial interventions are effective for reducing
fall rate by 23% for people at higher risk of falls but
no effect was found in studies that did not select for
people at higher risk of falls. Meta-analysis from
Caristia et al48 showed that multifactorial interventions lasting less than 12 months were effective in
reducing falls, while those lasting more than 12 months

were not. Cheng et al46 conducted a network metaanalysis (NMA) of the comparative effectiveness of
interventions and found multifactorial intervention
compared to usual care had the greatest efficacy
(36% reduced odds) relative to several other intervention comparisons including exercise, referral, and education. However, Cheng’s definition of multifactorial
intervention resulted in inclusion of multi-component
exercise interventions that likely caused overestimation
of the effect.

EXERCISE
Physical activity can be defined as any bodily movement
produced by skeletal muscles that results in energy
expenditure.52 Exercise is a type of physical activity featuring bodily movement that is planned, structured and
repetitive and is performed with the intention of improving or maintaining physical fitness.52 In this CPG, we
focus on exercise as opposed to physical activity, as
defined above. In 2018, the USPSTF released a final
statement recommending exercise to prevent falls in
older adults based on adequate evidence,50 and reissued
the recommendation in 2024.51 This has been supported

home hazards and strength/balance impairments, and should also include referral to appropriate providers for risk factors outside of PT
scope of practice. Provide risk-specific guidance regarding walking exercise programs for those at high risk.

Multicomponent Exercise Dosage: Provided in group or individual delivery format, for at least 3 hours/week and total volume > 50 hours
over 6-12 months. Must include balance training component.
Balance Training Dosage: Progressively reduce the BOS, movement of the body within and beyond the BOS through reaching, voluntary
stepping to adapt gait and prevent falling, and reactive stepping in response to an external perturbation to balance, reduce reliance on
upper limb support, 3+ hours/week and total volume of >50 hours.
Tai Chi Dosage: Provided 3+ times/week for a total volume of 30-60 hours.

Patient Population
This CPG addresses the management of falls and fall
risk in community-dwelling older adults. It is not
intended to address the management of falls and fall
risk in older adults who are institutionalized. Those
who are institutionalized may be at a greater risk of
falls but require care specific to the acute condition,
nursing home facility, or change in cognition, to name
a few examples. This CPG specifically defines community-dwelling older adults as 65 or over who do not
have major health conditions that prevent them from
interacting in their environment without substantial
physical, cognitive or social support. Clinicians should
use their clinical judgment for whether these recommendations apply to their patients that fall outside these

metadata.embedding_text:
Delivery personnel
In two high-quality SRs, Sherrington compared multicomponent interventions that were delivered by health
care professionals versus non-health care professionals,
and found no difference in fall rate or fall risk between
delivery by health care professionals and by non-health
care professionals.14,28 One low-quality SR without metaanalysis66 found that most physical therapist-led group
exercise programs reduced fall rates, but not more than
individualized physical therapy programs. These results
should be interpreted with caution as it is unclear if the
samples in these studies were similar enough to make
a direct comparison or were generalizable to a wider
population. For example, older adults who participate in
a community-based program delivered by a non-health
care professional might have less frailty or more ability
to exercise independently than those who participate in
programs delivered by a physical therapist or other health
care professional.

High-risk vs low-risk older adults
The evidence on the effect of multicomponent exercise on
older adults identified as being at a higher risk vs lower
risk of falling does not allow for separate recommendations. Gillespie et al34 found a similar reduction in fall rate
in studies that selected for people at high risk of falls and
in studies that did not (30% vs 28% rate reduction).
Sherrington et al14 also reported no differences between
studies that recruited older adults selected for high risk
and those that did not (24% vs 22% rate reduction,
respectively). In contrast, in one moderate-quality SR
that examined home-based individualized exercise programs, there was no effect on fall risk when including
studies of people who were recently discharged from the

hospital, but a 16% risk reduction when those studies
were excluded.61 Because this moderate quality study is
focused on home therapy alone, the GDG does not believe
that this study provides enough evidence of a differential
effect between people at higher and lower risk.

Two SRs with meta-analysis44,60 found large reductions in the fall rate and risk when including only studies
that recruited individuals with health conditions that
might impact falls. Liu et al,60 in a moderate quality
review that included only people with reduced physical
capacity, found a 37% reduction in fall rate, and Petridou
et al44 found an even larger 55% reduction in the fall risk
when examining studies that included only people with
a history of falls. Thus, we are unable to make separate
recommendations about high-risk individuals vs the general population and recommend that physical therapists
use clinical judgment based on individual patient examination of the movement system, patient safety, and
patient preferences.

participate in multifactorial management programs
addressing falls and fall risk for older adults. A multifactorial approach to fall risk management in older
adults is supported by robust evidence (Evidence
Quality/Level: I, Recommendation Strength: Strong).
A multicomponent exercise program that incorporates
balance training and other modes of exercise, such as
resistance training or Tai Chi, is strongly recommended
for reducing the risk and rate of falls (Evidence Quality/
Level: I, Recommendation Strength: Strong). The guideline
strongly recommends that balance training interventions
be progressive and sufficiently challenging, involve limb
and whole-body movements, changes in base of support,
and reduced upper limb support (Evidence Quality/Level: I,
Recommendation Strength: Strong). Additionally, Tai Chi
is strongly recommended for older adults in particular
those at lower fall risk (Evidence Quality/Level: I,
Recommendation Strength: Strong). The guideline makes
a strong recommendation for environmental assessments
and necessary modifications for older adults at higher risk
(Evidence Quality/Level: I, Recommendation Strength:
Strong). Providing or prescribing resistance training
ALONE to reduce fall risk and rate is not recommended,
as it offers limited benefits.(Evidence Quality/Level: II,
Recommendation Strength: Moderate).

This guideline also provides several weak recommendations. While reactive step (perturbation) training is
a potential component of balance training, the evidence
supporting this intervention is mixed (Evidence Quality/
Level: II, Recommendation Strength: Weak) in comparison to strong evidence for volitional step training or balance training. Additionally, this guideline recommends
a comprehensive approach that combines tailored education with individualized exercise intervention, addressing
identified risk factors, home hazards, strength and balance impairments, and referral to other providers when
necessary, especially for factors outside the scope of physical therapy (Evidence Quality/Level: V, Recommendation
Strength: Expert Opinion). The recommendation for this
comprehensive approach is predicated upon expert opinion, but each individual component is recommended
based upon robust evidence. These recommendations collectively guide physical therapists in adopting evidencebased practices to manage fall risk, while also highlighting
the limitations and areas requiring further research.

home hazards and strength/balance impairments, and should also include referral to appropriate providers for risk factors outside of PT

stepping to adapt gait and prevent falling, and reactive stepping in response to an external perturbation to balance, reduce reliance on
upper limb support, 3+ hours/week and total volume of >50 hours.
Tai Chi Dosage: Provided 3+ times/week for a total volume of 30-60 hours.

develop a clinical practice guideline (CPG) synthesizing the evidence for physical therapy management of fall risk in communitydwelling older adults. The GDG consisted of five physical therapists with clinical expertise in the management of fall risk in older
adults and methodological expertise in evidence-based document development. The CPG includes a systematic review of
existing literature, and stringent methodology developed by the
American Physical Therapy Association to form the evidencebased recommendations. The CPG content, including methodology, recommendations and algorithm were externally
reviewed by clinical providers and academicians with expertise in
fall risk management for older adults. These recommendations
are intended to assist physical therapists and physical therapist
assistants who are engaged in fall risk management for
community-dwelling older adults.
Key Words: fall risk, guidelines, older adults

(J Geriatr Phys Ther 2025;48(2):62-87.)

CLINICAL IMPLICATIONS
• Physical therapists can use the evidence-based algorithm to facilitate clinical reasoning in the management
of fall risk for older adults.
• Multicomponent exercise is the most important intervention for addressing falls and fall risk in older adults.
• Multicomponent exercise must include progressive and
challenging balance training exercises and may include
other types of exercise.

SUMMARY OF GRADED RECOMMENDATIONS
This clinical practice guideline (CPG) provides recommendations for the management of fall risk in communitydwelling adults aged 65 and over (subsequently referred
to as older adult(s)). Multifactorial management programs
include screening, assessment, referral to appropriate providers, and interventions within physical therapist (PT) and
physical therapist assistant (PTA) scope of practice. This
guideline strongly recommends that PTs and PTAs

Recommendation: Dosage, Intensity, and Components
Physical therapists must prescribe exercise programs to
older adults to be performed at least 150 minutes to
3 hours per week, lasting from 6 to 12 months, and
must include progressive and sufficiently challenging
balance training. (Evidence Quality/Level: I, Strength:
Strong)

Rationale
Multicomponent exercise programs that include more
than 150 minutes of exercise weekly are most effective
in reducing fall rates48 and programs of 6 to 12 months
duration are most effective in reducing fall rate and risk.60

Evidence from one meta-analysis61 examining the most
effective combination of exercises in studies with longer
follow-up times indicated that the most effective combination reduced risk by 35%, and included all categories of
exercise combined, including gait, balance, and functional
training, resistance training, flexibility exercises, and 3D
training such as Tai Chi or dance.

Evidence Synthesis
Duration, intensity, and components of mixed singleand multi-component exercise programs
In three separate SRs, Sherrington et al13,14,54 investigated
the intensity, duration, and components of mixed singleand multi-component exercise interventions and found
that the highest rate reductions were found with programs
that included high intensity/high challenge balance training, did not include walking programs, had doses greater
than 50 hours, and had frequencies greater than 3 hours
per week. Differences in fall risk and rate reduction
according to duration, intensity, or exercise components
are summarized in Table 7. The most recent high-quality
SR14 showed a 50% reduction in falls in programs that
included more than 3 hours per week and balance and
functional training.

Physical therapists must provide or prescribe multicomponent exercise to older adults to reduce risk and rate for

High-risk versus low-risk participants
Subgroup analyses from Gates et al43 revealed that
multifactorial interventions are effective for reducing

no effect was found in studies that did not select for

Caristia et al48 showed that multifactorial interventions lasting less than 12 months were effective in

were not. Cheng et al46 conducted a network metaanalysis (NMA) of the comparative effectiveness of
interventions and found multifactorial intervention
compared to usual care had the greatest efficacy
(36% reduced odds) relative to several other intervention comparisons including exercise, referral, and education. However, Cheng’s definition of multifactorial
intervention resulted in inclusion of multi-component
exercise interventions that likely caused overestimation
of the effect.

focus on exercise as opposed to physical activity, as

metadata.embedding_text:
Delivery personnel
In two high-quality SRs, Sherrington compared multicomponent interventions that were delivered by health
care professionals versus non-health care professionals,
and found no difference in fall rate or fall risk between
delivery by health care professionals and by non-health
care professionals.14,28 One low-quality SR without metaanalysis66 found that most physical therapist-led group
exercise programs reduced fall rates, but not more than
individualized physical therapy programs. These results
should be interpreted with caution as it is unclear if the
samples in these studies were similar enough to make
a direct comparison or were generalizable to a wider
population. For example, older adults who participate in
a community-based program delivered by a non-health
care professional might have less frailty or more ability
to exercise independently than those who participate in
programs delivered by a physical therapist or other health
care professional.

High-risk vs low-risk older adults
The evidence on the effect of multicomponent exercise on
older adults identified as being at a higher risk vs lower
risk of falling does not allow for separate recommendations. Gillespie et al34 found a similar reduction in fall rate
in studies that selected for people at high risk of falls and
in studies that did not (30% vs 28% rate reduction).
Sherrington et al14 also reported no differences between
studies that recruited older adults selected for high risk
and those that did not (24% vs 22% rate reduction,
respectively). In contrast, in one moderate-quality SR
that examined home-based individualized exercise programs, there was no effect on fall risk when including
studies of people who were recently discharged from the

hospital, but a 16% risk reduction when those studies
were excluded.61 Because this moderate quality study is
focused on home therapy alone, the GDG does not believe
that this study provides enough evidence of a differential
effect between people at higher and lower risk.

Two SRs with meta-analysis44,60 found large reductions in the fall rate and risk when including only studies
that recruited individuals with health conditions that
might impact falls. Liu et al,60 in a moderate quality
review that included only people with reduced physical
capacity, found a 37% reduction in fall rate, and Petridou
et al44 found an even larger 55% reduction in the fall risk
when examining studies that included only people with
a history of falls. Thus, we are unable to make separate
recommendations about high-risk individuals vs the general population and recommend that physical therapists
use clinical judgment based on individual patient examination of the movement system, patient safety, and
patient preferences.

participate in multifactorial management programs
addressing falls and fall risk for older adults. A multifactorial approach to fall risk management in older
adults is supported by robust evidence (Evidence
Quality/Level: I, Recommendation Strength: Strong).
A multicomponent exercise program that incorporates
balance training and other modes of exercise, such as
resistance training or Tai Chi, is strongly recommended
for reducing the risk and rate of falls (Evidence Quality/
Level: I, Recommendation Strength: Strong). The guideline
strongly recommends that balance training interventions
be progressive and sufficiently challenging, involve limb
and whole-body movements, changes in base of support,
and reduced upper limb support (Evidence Quality/Level: I,
Recommendation Strength: Strong). Additionally, Tai Chi
is strongly recommended for older adults in particular
those at lower fall risk (Evidence Quality/Level: I,
Recommendation Strength: Strong). The guideline makes
a strong recommendation for environmental assessments
and necessary modifications for older adults at higher risk
(Evidence Quality/Level: I, Recommendation Strength:
Strong). Providing or prescribing resistance training
ALONE to reduce fall risk and rate is not recommended,
as it offers limited benefits.(Evidence Quality/Level: II,
Recommendation Strength: Moderate).

This guideline also provides several weak recommendations. While reactive step (perturbation) training is
a potential component of balance training, the evidence
supporting this intervention is mixed (Evidence Quality/
Level: II, Recommendation Strength: Weak) in comparison to strong evidence for volitional step training or balance training. Additionally, this guideline recommends
a comprehensive approach that combines tailored education with individualized exercise intervention, addressing
identified risk factors, home hazards, strength and balance impairments, and referral to other providers when
necessary, especially for factors outside the scope of physical therapy (Evidence Quality/Level: V, Recommendation
Strength: Expert Opinion). The recommendation for this
comprehensive approach is predicated upon expert opinion, but each individual component is recommended
based upon robust evidence. These recommendations collectively guide physical therapists in adopting evidencebased practices to manage fall risk, while also highlighting
the limitations and areas requiring further research.

question: What are the key criteria for the clinical diagnosis of patellofemoral pain?
gold_answer: The guideline requires retropatellar or peripatellar pain; reproduction of that pain during activities that load the patellofemoral joint in flexion, such as squatting, stair climbing, or prolonged sitting; and exclusion of other causes of anterior knee pain.
gold_passage: “Clinicians should make the diagnosis of PFP using the following criteria: (1) the presence of retropatellar or peripatellar pain, (2) reproduction of retropatellar or peripatellar pain with squatting, stair climbing, prolonged sitting, or other functional activities loading the PFJ in a flexed position, and (3) exclusion of all other conditions that may cause anterior knee pain, including tibiofemoral pathologies.”

metadata.embedding_text:
Clinical Presentation
Patellofemoral pain is a common musculoskeletal-related
condition that is characterized by insidious onset of poorly
defined pain quality localized to the anterior retropatellar
and/or peripatellar region of the knee.80 The onset of symp
toms can be slow or acutely develop, with a worsening of pain
with lower-limb loading (eg, squatting, prolonged sitting, as
cending/descending stairs, jumping, or running, especially
with hills).154,234,254 While many pathoanatomic correlates,
such as internal derangement or cartilage softening, have
been offered from as early as 1928,106 all are poorly associated
with symptoms.94,254,288,291 Therefore, diagnosis is based on a
cluster of signs and symptoms after ruling out other patho
anatomic diagnoses.205 Because there is typically a progres
sive, insidious onset of symptoms, diagnosis is often delayed,
and describing the typical clinical course is difficult.

Pain
Collins et al61 conducted a retrospective review of 4 separate
studies on the presence of symptoms in 459 individuals with
PFP. They found that a large majority of these individuals re
ported at least some difficulty with squatting (93.7%), stair
negotiation (91.2%), and running (90.8%).61 People with PFP
tend to ascend and descend stairs with reduced knee flexion,

cpg10 | september 2019 | volume 49 | number 9 | journal of orthopaedic & sports physical therapy

and there is some debate as to whether this is consistently seen
in level walking.72 More than half (54.4%) of people with PFP
reported pain with prolonged sitting; another 26.4% reported
pain with sitting after exercise. Only 19.2% of people could sit
without pain.61 Pain with prolonged sitting had low to moder
ate diagnostic accuracy in an earlier systematic review.64

A systematic review of reviews concluded that AKP produced
by functional tasks such as squatting, stair climbing, and sit
ting with flexed knees is currently the best diagnostic indica
tor of PFP.222

Sandow and Goodfellow254 found less frequent reports of
symptoms with functional tasks in their long-term follow-up
of about 4 years, with 50% of participants reporting PFP on
a weekly or more frequent basis. Half of the cohort reported
pain with stair climbing and 39% with sport participation at
the 4-year follow-up. Although symptoms of PFP may become
less frequent over time, 94% still reported some degree of PFP,
either at rest or with other activities such as walking. Pain dur
ing running was not assessed.254 Sandow and Goodfellow254
also reported that nearly 50% of their cohort had bilateral PFP.

Clinicians should make the diagnosis of PFP using the fol
lowing criteria: (1) the presence of retropatellar or peri
patellar pain, (2) reproduction of retropatellar or peripatellar pain
with squatting, stair climbing, prolonged sitting, or other func
tional activities loading the PFJ in a flexed position, and (3) exclu
sion of all other conditions that may cause anterior knee pain,
including tibiofemoral pathologies.

Criteria for Considering Studies for Review
Inclusions: articles published in peer-reviewed journals that
include studies of the following types: systematic reviews, metaanalyses, experimental and quasi-experimental, cohort, case
series, and cross-sectional studies.

Inclusion Criteria
Articles reporting on
• The functional anatomy of the patellofemoral joint
OR
• Tests and measures for diagnosis and/or differential diagnosis
of patellofemoral pain within the scope of physical therapist
practice, including but not limited to “specific tests and
measures”
OR
• Measurement properties of instruments and tests specific to
measuring patellofemoral pain, or patellofemoral pain–related
outcomes (including but not limited to symptoms, functions,
activity, and participation)
OR
• Measurement properties of instruments that are specific to
patellofemoral pain or lower extremity outcomes tested in pa
tients with patellofemoral pain
OR
• Measurement properties of instruments using data from a
sample of patients with patellofemoral pain
OR
• Primarily adolescents (12 years of age or older) and adults with
patellofemoral pain
- Studies reporting on persons younger than 12 years of age

Component 2
Differential evaluation of musculoskeletal clinical findings
determines the most relevant physical impairments associat
ed with the patient’s reported activity limitations and medical
diagnosis.157 Clusters of these clinical findings are described
as impairment patterns in the physical therapy literature,
and are labeled according to the key impairment(s) of body
function associated with that cluster. The authors propose a
classification system for PFP, with subcategories named ac
cording to the primary impairments. These impairment-pat
tern subcategories for PFP are described in the Diagnosis and
Classification sections of this CPG. The ICD-10 and primary
and secondary ICF codes associated with PFP are provided
in the Methods section of this CPG. These impairment pat
terns impact the selection of interventions, which focus on
normalizing the key impairments of body function, which in
turn should improve the movement and function of the pa
tient and lessen or alleviate the activity limitations commonly
reported by the patients who meet the diagnostic criteria of
that specific pattern. The FIGURE lists the key clinical findings
used to rule in or rule out the common impairment patterns
and their associated medical conditions. Impairment-based
classification is critical for matching the intervention strat
egy that is most likely to provide the optimal outcome for
a patient’s clinical findings.157 However, it is important for
clinicians to understand that the impairment pattern, the
most relevant impairments of body function, and the associ
ated intervention strategies often change during the patient’s
episode of care. Thus, continual re-evaluation of the patient’s
response to treatment and the patient’s emerging clinical
findings is important for providing optimal interventions
throughout the patient’s episode of care.28

Component 3
Irritability is a term used by rehabilitation practitioners to
reflect the tissue’s ability to handle physical stress,190,200 and is
presumably related to physical status and the extent of injury
and inflammatory activity that is present. McClure and Mi

ity for persons with shoulder pain that could be used to guide
intensity and selection of interventions. These include high,
moderate, and low irritability levels, which are characterized
by pain intensity and disability level, as well as provocation of

Inclusions: articles published in peer-reviewed journals that
include studies of the following types: systematic reviews, metaanalyses, experimental and quasi-experimental, cohort, case
series, and cross-sectional studies.

Inclusion Criteria
Articles reporting on
• The functional anatomy of the patellofemoral joint
OR
• Tests and measures for diagnosis and/or differential diagnosis
of patellofemoral pain within the scope of physical therapist
practice, including but not limited to “specific tests and
measures”
OR
• Measurement properties of instruments and tests specific to
measuring patellofemoral pain, or patellofemoral pain–related
outcomes (including but not limited to symptoms, functions,
activity, and participation)
OR
• Measurement properties of instruments that are specific to
patellofemoral pain or lower extremity outcomes tested in pa
tients with patellofemoral pain
OR
• Measurement properties of instruments using data from a
sample of patients with patellofemoral pain
OR
• Primarily adolescents (12 years of age or older) and adults with
patellofemoral pain
- Studies reporting on persons younger than 12 years of age

Clinicians should make the diagnosis of PFP using the fol
lowing criteria: (1) the presence of retropatellar or peri
patellar pain, (2) reproduction of retropatellar or peripatellar pain
with squatting, stair climbing, prolonged sitting, or other func
tional activities loading the PFJ in a flexed position, and (3) exclu
sion of all other conditions that may cause anterior knee pain,
including tibiofemoral pathologies.

Extensive literature searches identified 11,905 citations potentially addressing the key questions
of interest to this evidence review. Of those, 9,413 were excluded upon title review for clearly
not meeting inclusion criteria (e.g., not pertinent to the topic, not published in English, published
prior to study inclusion publication date, or not a full-length article). Overall, 2,492 abstracts
were reviewed with 2,290 of those being excluded for the following reasons: not a systematic
review or clinical study, did not address a key question of interest to this review, did not enroll a
population of interest, or published prior to July 6, 2016. A total of 202 full-length articles were
reviewed. Of those, 100 were excluded at a first pass review for the following: not addressing a
key question of interest, not enrolling the population of interest, not meeting inclusion criteria for
clinical study or systematic review, not meeting inclusion criteria for any key question, or being a
duplicate. A total of 102 full-length articles were thought to address one or more key questions
and were further reviewed. Of these, 66 were ultimately excluded. Reasons for their exclusion
are presented in Figure A-1 below.

Overall, 36 publications addressed one or more of the Key Questions and were considered as
evidence in this review. Table A-4 indicates the number of studies that addressed each of the
KQs.

DECISION TREE MODEL
A pathoanatomical/medical diagnosis of PFP can provide
valuable information in describing tissue pathology and may
assist in nonoperative planning and prognosis. The proposed
model for examination, diagnosis, and treatment planning
for patients with PFP uses the following components: (1)
medical screening, (2) classification of the condition through
evaluation of clinical findings suggestive of musculoskeletal
impairments of body functioning (ICF) and associated tis
sue pathology/disease (ICD), (3) determination of irritability
stage and psychosocial factors that may impact treatment, (4)
evaluative outcome measures, and (5) nonoperative interven
tion strategies. This model is depicted in the FIGURE.

Component 1
Medical screening incorporates the findings of the history
and physical examination to determine whether the patient’s
symptoms originate from a condition that requires referral
to another health care provider. Prior to diagnosing a person
with PFP, it is necessary to rule out all other possible medical
conditions that may cause AKP. Clinicians should recognize

the key signs and symptoms associated with serious patho
logical knee conditions, continually screen for the presence
of these conditions throughout treatment, and immediately
initiate referral to the appropriate medical practitioner when
a potentially serious medical condition is suspected (Guide
to Physical Therapist Practice 3.0; http://guidetoptpractice.
apta.org/). Medical conditions for which physical therapy is
not indicated must be considered as possible etiologies of a
patient’s symptoms.

Document Structure and
Scope of the CPG
The key action statements are organized in Table 4 with
their assigned recommendation grade, followed by a
standardized content outline that was generated by
BRIDGE-Wiz software (http://gem.med.yale.edu/BRIDGEWiz/). The key action statements are organized with a
content title that addresses the specifics of the statement,
a recommendation of an observable action, the evidence
quality for the key action statement, and strength of the
recommendation. Each action statement describes the: (1)
benefits, harms, and potential costs associated with the
recommendation, (2) delineation of the assumptions or
judgments in formatting the recommendation, (3)
potential reasons for intentional vagueness within the
recommendation, (4) role of patient preferences, and (5)
exclusions. Each key action statement is then followed by
a summary of evidence to highlight the interpretation of
evidence, justify the strength of recommendation, and
assist clinicians with implementation of the key action
statement. The GDG regularly met for extensive
discussion based on data extracted in the evidence
summary tables to reach consensus regarding each key
action statement. Much of the variability in considering
the strength of evidence for a guideline was eliminated for
the GDG with the inclusion of only systematic reviews
and meta-analyses of RCTs. When discussions about
evidence did occur, they were based on easily identified
criteria within the evidence summary tables, such as the
number of subjects, number of trials, study criteria, and
patient characteristic, and were therefore easily resolved.

Informing the Diagnostic Process for Developmental
Coordination Disorder
metadata.embedding_text:
DCD is defined as a neurodevelopmental disorder and subcate
gorized as a motor disorder in the DSM-5-TR.6 According to the
DSM-5-TR, all 4 diagnostic components (Criteria A through D)
must be met to confirm a diagnosis of DCD. Table 4 lists the
required DSM-5-TR diagnostic criteria.

There is consensus that diagnosis and management of DCD
requires an interprofessional team approach.40,41 This team may
include the child and caregivers, the primary care provider, pedi
atric psychiatrists and neurologists, PTs, occupational therapists,
speech-language pathologists, and other relevant service provid
ers. Service coordination and collaboration are crucial to address
function, participation, and the prevention of secondary conse
quences, while maintaining a child-centered and family-informed
approach. Children diagnosed with DCD should also be screened
for co-occurring conditions, such as ADHD and ASD.42 Pediatric
PTs contribute their expertise in child development, motor con
trol, motor learning, movement observation, functional training,
and clinical reasoning. They often serve as key advocates and
coordinators in both clinical and educational settings.

While PTs in the United States are not licensed to inde
pendently diagnose DCD, data gathered during a comprehen
sive physical therapy examination can contribute meaningfully
to the diagnostic process. This data may support other findings
used by a multidisciplinary team, inclusive of a PT, to arrive at
a diagnosis.1,6,8,43 A formal diagnosis of DCD is typically made
when a child is 5 years of age or older, as the diagnostic criteria
can be more accurately applied then; however, signs of motor
coordination difficulties may be evident much earlier.

can be more accurately applied then; however, signs of motor
coordination difficulties may be evident much earlier.

Criteria for Considering Studies for Review
Inclusions: articles published in peer-reviewed journals that
include studies of the following types: systematic reviews, metaanalyses, experimental and quasi-experimental, cohort, case
series, and cross-sectional studies.

Inclusion Criteria
Articles reporting on
• The functional anatomy of the patellofemoral joint
OR
• Tests and measures for diagnosis and/or differential diagnosis
of patellofemoral pain within the scope of physical therapist
practice, including but not limited to “specific tests and
measures”
OR
• Measurement properties of instruments and tests specific to
measuring patellofemoral pain, or patellofemoral pain–related
outcomes (including but not limited to symptoms, functions,
activity, and participation)
OR
• Measurement properties of instruments that are specific to
patellofemoral pain or lower extremity outcomes tested in pa
tients with patellofemoral pain
OR
• Measurement properties of instruments using data from a
sample of patients with patellofemoral pain
OR
• Primarily adolescents (12 years of age or older) and adults with
patellofemoral pain
- Studies reporting on persons younger than 12 years of age

Clinicians should use reproduction of retropatellar or peri
patellar pain during squatting as a diagnostic test for
patellofemoral pain (PFP). Clinicians should also use perfor
mance of other functional activities that load the patellofemoral
joint (PFJ) in a flexed position, such as stair climbing or descent,
as diagnostic tests for PFP.

metadata.embedding_text:
Clinical Presentation
Patellofemoral pain is a common musculoskeletal-related
condition that is characterized by insidious onset of poorly
defined pain quality localized to the anterior retropatellar
and/or peripatellar region of the knee.80 The onset of symp
toms can be slow or acutely develop, with a worsening of pain
with lower-limb loading (eg, squatting, prolonged sitting, as
cending/descending stairs, jumping, or running, especially
with hills).154,234,254 While many pathoanatomic correlates,
such as internal derangement or cartilage softening, have
been offered from as early as 1928,106 all are poorly associated
with symptoms.94,254,288,291 Therefore, diagnosis is based on a
cluster of signs and symptoms after ruling out other patho
anatomic diagnoses.205 Because there is typically a progres
sive, insidious onset of symptoms, diagnosis is often delayed,
and describing the typical clinical course is difficult.

Pain
Collins et al61 conducted a retrospective review of 4 separate
studies on the presence of symptoms in 459 individuals with
PFP. They found that a large majority of these individuals re
ported at least some difficulty with squatting (93.7%), stair
negotiation (91.2%), and running (90.8%).61 People with PFP
tend to ascend and descend stairs with reduced knee flexion,

cpg10 | september 2019 | volume 49 | number 9 | journal of orthopaedic & sports physical therapy

and there is some debate as to whether this is consistently seen
in level walking.72 More than half (54.4%) of people with PFP
reported pain with prolonged sitting; another 26.4% reported
pain with sitting after exercise. Only 19.2% of people could sit
without pain.61 Pain with prolonged sitting had low to moder
ate diagnostic accuracy in an earlier systematic review.64

A systematic review of reviews concluded that AKP produced
by functional tasks such as squatting, stair climbing, and sit
ting with flexed knees is currently the best diagnostic indica
tor of PFP.222

Sandow and Goodfellow254 found less frequent reports of
symptoms with functional tasks in their long-term follow-up
of about 4 years, with 50% of participants reporting PFP on
a weekly or more frequent basis. Half of the cohort reported
pain with stair climbing and 39% with sport participation at
the 4-year follow-up. Although symptoms of PFP may become
less frequent over time, 94% still reported some degree of PFP,
either at rest or with other activities such as walking. Pain dur
ing running was not assessed.254 Sandow and Goodfellow254
also reported that nearly 50% of their cohort had bilateral PFP.

Component 2
Differential evaluation of musculoskeletal clinical findings
determines the most relevant physical impairments associat
ed with the patient’s reported activity limitations and medical
diagnosis.157 Clusters of these clinical findings are described
as impairment patterns in the physical therapy literature,
and are labeled according to the key impairment(s) of body
function associated with that cluster. The authors propose a
classification system for PFP, with subcategories named ac
cording to the primary impairments. These impairment-pat
tern subcategories for PFP are described in the Diagnosis and
Classification sections of this CPG. The ICD-10 and primary
and secondary ICF codes associated with PFP are provided
in the Methods section of this CPG. These impairment pat
terns impact the selection of interventions, which focus on
normalizing the key impairments of body function, which in
turn should improve the movement and function of the pa
tient and lessen or alleviate the activity limitations commonly
reported by the patients who meet the diagnostic criteria of
that specific pattern. The FIGURE lists the key clinical findings
used to rule in or rule out the common impairment patterns
and their associated medical conditions. Impairment-based
classification is critical for matching the intervention strat
egy that is most likely to provide the optimal outcome for
a patient’s clinical findings.157 However, it is important for
clinicians to understand that the impairment pattern, the
most relevant impairments of body function, and the associ
ated intervention strategies often change during the patient’s
episode of care. Thus, continual re-evaluation of the patient’s
response to treatment and the patient’s emerging clinical
findings is important for providing optimal interventions
throughout the patient’s episode of care.28

Component 3
Irritability is a term used by rehabilitation practitioners to
reflect the tissue’s ability to handle physical stress,190,200 and is
presumably related to physical status and the extent of injury
and inflammatory activity that is present. McClure and Mi
chener190 proposed operational definitions for tissue irritabil
ity for persons with shoulder pain that could be used to guide
intensity and selection of interventions. These include high,

Clinicians should use information from the patient’s age,
history, provocative activities, and physical examination test
results to screen for the presence of other possible causes of
AKP.43,293 Pain from patellar tendinopathy is typically local
ized to the inferior pole of the patella or near the tibial tu
bercle.188 Patellar tendinopathy may be differentiated from
PFP by pain located over the patellar tendon, tenderness to
palpation of the patellar tendon, and symptom response. Pain
from patellar tendinopathy is aggravated by activities that
require higher rates of knee extensor loading, such as jump
ing (eg, basketball, volleyball) or high-speed sprinting (eg,
football/soccer).188 If patellar instability or a history of patel
lar dislocation is suspected from subjective interview, then
reported apprehension with passively applied lateral patellar movement (a positive apprehension test) may provide confir
mation.162 Clinicians should refer to the consensus statement
written by the international patellofemoral osteoarthritis
consortium for clinical symptoms and signs to screen for the
presence of PFOA.293 Anterior knee pain in children may be due to apophysitis of
the tibial tubercle (Osgood-Schlatter disease) or the inferior
pole of the patella (Sinding-Larsen-Johansson disease).317,318
Clinicians should use the patient’s age and the presence
of tenderness to palpation over the tibial tubercle or infe
rior pole of the patella to determine the presence of these
conditions.316 Patellofemoral pain may be experienced following surgical
procedures, for example, anterior cruciate ligament recon
struction (ACLR).76,77 Although PFP is common in persons
following ACLR, this may present differently from nonsur
gical PFP due to alterations in the normal knee biomechan
ics.77 This guideline does not apply to PFP following surgery
to the knee or other musculoskeletal regions of the lower
extremity.

Extensive literature searches identified 11,905 citations potentially addressing the key questions
of interest to this evidence review. Of those, 9,413 were excluded upon title review for clearly
not meeting inclusion criteria (e.g., not pertinent to the topic, not published in English, published
prior to study inclusion publication date, or not a full-length article). Overall, 2,492 abstracts
were reviewed with 2,290 of those being excluded for the following reasons: not a systematic
review or clinical study, did not address a key question of interest to this review, did not enroll a
population of interest, or published prior to July 6, 2016. A total of 202 full-length articles were
reviewed. Of those, 100 were excluded at a first pass review for the following: not addressing a
key question of interest, not enrolling the population of interest, not meeting inclusion criteria for
clinical study or systematic review, not meeting inclusion criteria for any key question, or being a
duplicate. A total of 102 full-length articles were thought to address one or more key questions
and were further reviewed. Of these, 66 were ultimately excluded. Reasons for their exclusion
are presented in Figure A-1 below.

Overall, 36 publications addressed one or more of the Key Questions and were considered as
evidence in this review. Table A-4 indicates the number of studies that addressed each of the
KQs.
